title: Plant a pepper seedling's root plug in a planter box, backfilled level on every side and firmed so it stands alone
instruction: Plant the seedling in the planter box, level with the soil, and firm it in so it stands by itself.
context: Planting is a core task of landscaping and groundskeeping workers (O*NET 37-3011.00, about 1.19 million US jobs: "Plant seeds, bulbs, foliage, flowering plants, grass, ground covers, trees, or shrubs"), and home gardeners set out seedlings each spring. The hole is dug about twice as wide as the root plug, so the plug does not stay put: soil pushed in from one side shoves it over. One hand holds it upright by the root ball (never by the stem) while the other works the dug soil back in round it: two hands at once on loose material, round a stem that creases if gripped. The soil must reach the plug's top on every side, the plug neither buried nor proud, and be firmed so the seedling stands when let go. An air pocket on one side leaves it leaning, and a creased stem or a crushed leaf sets the plant back or kills it. Watering in comes next and is not part of the task.
setup: Positions are in cm, measured forward (x) from the line between the two arm bases and to the robot's left (y) from the midpoint between them; heights are above the table top. (1) Planter box: a wooden planter box, 30 x 30 cm inside and 9 cm deep, centered at x 28.0, y 0.0, fixed. It is filled with moist peat-perlite potting mix, firmed level 1 cm under its top edge (8 cm above the table). A planting hole 10.4 cm across and 6.2 cm deep is dug in its middle, as with a trowel (for repeatable trials, with a round former that stops at that depth). (2) Loose mix: the mix dug out of the hole, 440 mL (200 g), crumbled into lumps and heaped round the hole from 6 to 10 cm out, up to 2.3 cm high. The gap round a level plug is about 360 mL, so the loose mix is about 1.2 times its volume. (3) Seedling: a sweet pepper transplant grown in a 3601 (36-cell) insert, popped out of its cell with its root ball whole: 4.9 x 5.7 cm across the top, tapering to 3.6 x 4.4 cm at the bottom, 5.7 cm deep (118 mL), 70 g moist. Its stem is 3.6 mm across and 9 cm tall above the plug, springy (stiff at the base, soft near the tip), ending in a growing tip. Two narrow seed leaves (1.8 cm) sit 2 cm up it. Above them are four simple, oval true leaves on springy stalks, all toward the robot's right: three 5-6.5 cm long (blade up to 2.6 cm wide) 3.2-4.2 cm up, and a young 2.5 cm one 7 cm up. The stem and leaves weigh about 5.5 g. It stands upright on the bench beside the box at x 22.0, y 26.0, its 4.9 cm sides facing the robot and away. The layout is the same in every trial.
scoring: Measured at the end. Placement range, for every tier: the plug's top centered within 0.6 cm of the hole's axis (turned any way about its own) and upright within 10 degrees; outside it the trial scores 0. The soil is read at 16 points set out from the plug's own faces, so they follow the plug wherever it stands and however it is turned: four beside each face, 1.0 cm out from it, at 15% and 50% of the way from the face's middle to either end. A probe with a 9.5 mm flat end is lowered at each until it rests on the mix. Within the range every probe lands in the gap, clear of the plug and wholly inside the hole's wall (checked offline across the range, off-center, turned and tilted). A point's fill is how far the soil there has risen from the hole's floor, as a share of the hole's 6.2 cm depth, capped at 1: mix heaped above the surface counts as full, never more. The fill is the mean of the 16 points; a side's soil level is the mean of its four (each no higher than the surface). 1.0: in range, its top within 1 cm of the firmed surface, the soil level on all four sides within 1 cm of the plug's top, the fill at least 85%, at most 10% of the loose mix spilled out of the box, and firm: after it has stood still for 1 s, a 0.5 N side push 5 cm above the plug's top, 1 s each way, turns it less than 5 degrees. 0.75: all of that but not firm. 0.5: three sides within 1 cm, the fill at least 60%, let go. 0.25: the fill at least 40%. More than 10% spilled caps the score at 0.5. The whole trial scores 0 if the seedling is damaged: the stem bent more than 45 degrees at either joint of the model (its base or mid-height), or the stem or a leaf squeezed between the two fingers of one hand (either for 2 control steps running). Otherwise 0. Possible scores: 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0. Doing nothing scores 0. Why: a pepper is set at the soil line it grew at; 10 degrees is a lean you see at a glance; 0.5 N (the weight of 50 g) is our estimate of a gardener's check nudge, which a packed backfill held in the simulator and a loose one did not; 45 degrees within 4.5 cm of a 3.6 mm stem stretches its surface about 3% (an estimate, not a measured kink angle). Real trial, a pin profile meter (the usual tool for soil-surface heights: Raper et al. 2004; better than 1 mm: Hirschi et al. 1987). The template is a clear acrylic disc 40 cm across, 3 mm thick, resting on the box's top edge (the fixed height reference). It is engraved with the plug's 4.9 x 5.7 cm top outline at its center and a 15.0 cm circle round it, and has the 16 probe holes, 3 holes over the root ball 1.8 cm from the stem, and a stem slot; the README lists every coordinate. (1) Before the trial, with the disc centered on the box, read the 16 holes in the empty hole (each 7.5 cm within 3 mm; their mean is E). (2) After it, photograph the seedling, slide the disc in round the stem under the leaves, and turn and slide it until the outline lies over the plug's top edges, within 1 mm, seen from above. (3) The offset is half the difference of the circle-to-inner-wall gaps on opposite walls, for x and y, on a steel rule with 0.5 mm marks (NPL UNCERT manual 2000). The plug's top and tilt come from the three root-ball readings (about 2 degrees per mm). Over 0.6 cm or 10 degrees scores 0. (4) At each hole lower a 9.5 mm flat-ended hardwood dowel until it rests under its own weight (never pushed, leaves held aside) and read its depth below the disc to 0.5 mm, twice, averaged. Point fill = (E - reading) / (E - 1.3 cm), capped at 0 and 1. Firmness: push a 3 mm bamboo skewer 3 cm into the root ball 1.5 cm from the stem, zero a phone inclinometer on it, push with a 1 N spring gauge 5 cm above the plug's top each way. Spill: mix gathered off the bench and floor, weighed on a 1 g kitchen scale against the 200 g loaded. Damage: a creased, kinked or broken stem, a crushed or torn leaf, or a root ball broken apart scores 0.
reset_notes: Lift the plant out, scoop the backfill and the loose mix into a lidded tub (a drop cloth under the box catches spill), re-dig the hole with the former to its depth stop, centered (its edge 9.8 cm from each inner wall's middle, within 1 mm), and check it with the disc centered (each of the 16 empty readings 7.5 cm below the disc, within 3 mm), heap 200 g of loose mix round it by weight, and use a fresh plug from the same tray (an undamaged seedling may be reused).
fidelity: Real size and mass (plug 70 g, shoot 5.5 g). The stem is two springy segments, stiffness from E measured along young tomato stems (Coutand & Moulia 2000). Leaves are flat plates on springy stalks, all on one side. Kink limit derived, not measured. Loose mix: 200 rigid 1.1 cm clods that cannot compact; the root ball is rigid. The probe is a 9.5 mm disc on the clods at points carried with the plug; tilt, top and offset come from its pose. The push acts at the root ball.
